# Lab 10: App Admin {.unnumbered} :::: {.callout-warning collapse='false' appearance='default' icon='false'} ## [Caution]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.25em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.00em; color: var(--callout-body-color, #282b2d);'} This section is being revised. Thank you for your patience. ::: :::: This lab covers installing Linux packages, daemonizing an application with `systemd`, and working with text files and editors from the command line. ## Comprehension questions > "*What are two different ways to install Linux applications, and what are the commands?*" My instance is Amazon Linux 2, so the system package manager is `yum`, not Ubuntu's `apt`: * `sudo yum install ` pulls a package (and its dependencies) from AL2's configured repositories. * `sudo yum update` keeps everything already installed current. * For software that isn't in the repos, I download the package myself with `wget ` and install it directly: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo yum localinstall .rpm # or sudo rpm -i .rpm ``` ::: * No dependency resolution beyond what's already on the box, so this is my second choice, not my first. > "*What does it mean to daemonize a Linux application? What programs and commands are used to do so?*" Daemonizing an application means running it as a background service that starts on boot, restarts if it crashes, and keeps running independent of any login session, instead of a process that dies the moment I close my SSH connection. On AL2, `systemd` is the program that manages this, and `systemctl` is how I talk to it: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Daemonizing with systemd' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"12px"}}}%% graph TD subgraph Unit["Unit File"] DotService["/etc/systemd/system/*.service"] end Reload("systemctl daemon-reload") Enable("systemctl enable
starts on boot") Start("systemctl start") Status("systemctl status") Unit --> Reload --> Enable --> Start --"running now"--> Status style DotService stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#000,font-family:monospace,font-size:11px style Unit fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Reload fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff,font-family:monospace,font-size:14px style Enable fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff,font-family:monospace style Start fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff,font-family:monospace style Status fill:#E8A33D,stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px,color:#000,font-family:monospace ``` Once the unit file exists, `systemctl restart` and `systemctl stop` manage it going forward, and `systemctl disable` stops it from starting on boot. ### Anatomy of a unit file A unit file is a short INI style text file with three sections: ```{.default} [Unit] Description= After=network.target [Service] User= WorkingDirectory= ExecStart= Restart=on-failure [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target ``` `[Unit]` describes the service and what it waits for (`After=network.target` holds it until networking is up). `[Service]` says how to run it: which account it runs as (`User=`), where it starts (`WorkingDirectory=`), the exact command (`ExecStart=`), and what to do when it exits (`Restart=`). `[Install]` says when to start it on boot; `multi-user.target` is the normal booted state of a server. `systemd` runs `ExecStart` directly, with no shell, no `PATH` search, and no virtual environment activation. Anything an interactive session quietly provides has to be spelled out in the unit file, which is why the path is always absolute. After `systemctl enable --now `, I never assume the service is running. `systemctl status ` shows the state (`active (running)`) and whether it starts on boot (`enabled`), and `journalctl -u ` shows the service's output when something goes wrong. [Installing a Real Application](install-real-app.qmd) walks through all of this for a real app, from the unit file to reading a failed start. > "*How do you know if you've opened Nano or Vim? How would you exit them if you didn’t mean to?*" Nano tells me right away: the bottom of the screen fills with a menu of keybindings (`^X Exit`, `^O Write Out`, etc.), and I can just start typing. Vim gives no such hints: it opens in **normal mode**, the screen is otherwise blank (empty lines marked with `~`), and typing does nothing useful until I switch to **insert mode**. That silence is usually how I know I've landed in Vim by accident. To back out without changing anything: **Nano**: `Ctrl + X`, then answer `N` if it asks whether to save ![](img/lab10-nano.png){width='100%'} **Vim**: press `Esc` first to make sure I'm in normal mode (not typing into the file), then type `:q!` and hit `Enter` to quit and discard any changes. ![](img/lab10-vim.png){width='100%'} > *"What are four commands to read text files?"* `cat`, `less`, `head`, and `tail`. I reach for `cat` on short files, `less` for anything long enough to scroll, `head` when I only need the first lines, and `tail -f` when I want to watch a log file update in real time. > "*How would you create a file called secrets.txt, open it with Vim, write something in, close and save it, and make it so that only you can read it?*" ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} vim secrets.txt ``` ::: From there: 1. Press `i` to enter insert mode and type the content. 2. Press `Esc` to return to normal mode. 3. Type `:wq` and hit `Enter` to write (save) and quit. Then lock it down so only I can read it: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} chmod 600 secrets.txt ``` ::: `600` gives the owner read/write and removes every permission for group and other; it's the same restriction I already use on `.ssh/authorized_keys` in [Linux Users](linux-users.qmd). ## Recap 1. On Amazon Linux 2, `sudo yum install` pulls a package and its dependencies from the configured repositories. A downloaded `.rpm` installed with `yum localinstall` or `rpm -i` is my second choice, because it can't lean on the repositories for dependencies. 2. Daemonizing hands the app to `systemd`: write a unit file in `/etc/systemd/system`, then run `systemctl daemon-reload` and `systemctl enable --now`. `User=`, an absolute `ExecStart` path, and `Restart=on-failure` do most of the work, because `systemd` runs the command with no shell. 3. `enable --now` only means `systemd` tried. I confirm with `systemctl status` (looking for `active (running)` and `enabled`) and read `journalctl -u ` when it fails. 4. Nano shows its keybindings and exits with `Ctrl + X`; Vim opens silently in normal mode and exits without saving with `Esc`, then `:q!`. `chmod 600` makes a file like `secrets.txt` readable only by its owner. [Install Apps](install-apps.qmd) covers `PATH` and installing language runtimes into `/opt`, and [Installing a Real Application](install-real-app.qmd) installs `baseball-trajectory` and runs it as a `systemd` service.
